input: Given question: A patient visits you complaining of decreased deltoid function. You conclude that they have suffered damage to their axillary nerve. The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space, the lateral border of which is formed by the humerus. What forms the medial border? Option A: Inferior border of subscapularis Option B: Inferior border of teres minor Option C: Long head of triceps brachii Option D: Short head of biceps brachii Option E: Superior border of teres major The correct answer is Option C.
reference:
https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/areas/quadrangular-space/ - has a good summary and some nice images.https://open.oregonstate.education/aandp/chapter/14-5-the-axillary-nerve/ - has some good info on axillary nerve innervated muscles.https://www.anatomystuff.co.uk/repository/products/user/img_img_9781587799259_disorders_of_the_shoulder_joseph_carlo_guise_63827_.jpg - appears to be a photo of the quadrangular space, maybe useful? (It's from this website: https://www.anatomystuff.co.uk/shop/en/ Shoulder%20Anatomy)
===============================================================================================================================The quadrangular space is located in the shoulder region and is bounded by four structures: the axillary nerve, the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein, and the long and short heads of the biceps brachii. The axillary nerve is the most medial structure and separates the quadrangular space from the teres major muscle. The long head of the triceps brachii is the most lateral structure and separates the quadrangular space from the teres minor muscle. The short head of the biceps brachii is located within the quadrangular space, as is the coracobrachialis muscle. The main artery and vein enter the quadrangular space superior to the teres major muscle and exit inferior to the teres minor muscle. Around the axilla, the fasciae of the upper limb emerge from the underlying trapezius muscle. They are thin and transparent and surround the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein. Their borders correspond to the boundaries of the quadrangular space. The artery and vein pass across the quadrangular space to reach the region around the elbow. The axillary nerve passes with them, but turns medially towards the teres major muscle. It then moves laterally along the posterior boundary of the quadrangular space to rejoin its continuation in the brachial plexus at the lateral cord. The anterior boundary of the quadrangular space is formed by the coracoid process of the scapula and the shaft of the humerus. The posterior boundary is marked by an imaginary line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus. The superior boundary is defined by an oblique line joining the superior angle of the scapula to the inferior margin of the teres major muscle. The inferior boundary is formed by an imaginary horizontal line connecting the inferior angles of the scapula. The quadrangular space contains the axillary nerve, the long and short heads of the biceps brachii, the coracobrachialis muscle, and the deep brachial artery and vein. The space is separated from the teres major muscle by the axillary nerve and from the teres minor muscle by the long head of the triceps brachii. The space is also separated from the shaft of the humerus by the axillary nerve and the deep brachial artery and vein. The quadrangular space communicates with the following structures:the deltoid muscle, which covers it superiorly.the teres major muscle, which covers it inferiorly.the supraspinatus ables, which lies against the superior boundary.the infraspinatus and teres minor muscles, which lie against the inferior boundary.the brachial artery and vein, which pass through it.the axillary nerve, which lies within it.the coracobrachialis muscle, which lies within it.the long head of the triceps brachii, which separates it from the teres minor muscle.the short head of the biceps brachii, which lies within it.the shaft of the humerus, which is separated from it by the axillary nerve and the deep brachial artery and vein.https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/areas/quadrangular-space/ - has a good summary and some nice images.https://open.oregonstate.education/aandp/chapter/14-5-the-axillary-nerve/ - has some good info on axillary nerve innervated mus

The axillary nerve is vulnerable to damage from shoulder surgery or traction if the shoulder is dislocated. input: Given question: Which glucose transporter acts as a glucose sensor, stimulating the release of insulin when required? Option A: GLUT 1 Option B: GLUT 2 Option C: GLUT 3 Option D: GLUT 4 Option E: GLUT 5 The correct answer is Option B.
reference: GLUT 1 - found in beta cells and has low affinity for glucose. It helps to maintain a high concentration of glucose within the beta cell.  GLUT 2 - found in the liver, pancreatic alpha cells and the brain. It has a high affinity for glucose and when blood glucose is high, acts as a glucose sensor, stimulating the release of insulin from the beta cells.  GLUT 3 - found everywhere! It has a relatively low affinity for glucose but once bound, releases glucose very rapidly. This transporter therefore acts as an energy source for cells.  GLUT 4 - this comes on stream when exercise is continued over a prolonged period of time. It has an even higher affinity for glucose than GLUT 2 and stimulates the uptake of glucose in muscle.  GLUT 5 - this transporter is involved in the transport of fructose. It is not stimulated by increases in blood glucose.  Source: Medical Biochemistry by Baynes and Dominiczak (ISBN 978-1-84846-200-9) and Dr Allen's lecture on 'Insulin and Glucagon: Mechanisms of Action’.  This is an open-access document available at http://www.mcb.harvard.edu/mitosis/glossary/transport_01.html#bottomline   The diagram below shows where each GLUT transporter is expressed:  +-------------------+ +-----------------+ +------------+ +----------+ +------------+ +----------+ +-----------------+ +-------------------+  Pancreatic Beta Cell  Liver  Kidney  Heart  Skeletal Muscle  Blood Brain  Retina  Lens  +-------------------+ +-----------------+ GLUT 1  GLUT 2  GLUT 3  GLUT 4  GLUT 5  +------------+ +----------+ +------------+ +----------+ +-----------------+ +-------------------+ Note that GLUT 5 is the only one of these transporters which is activated by fructose, rather than glucose.  Also note that GLUT 2 is the transporter which senses changes in blood glucose levels and stimulates the release of insulin from the beta cells.  TJ Allen's lecture mentions that people with type 2 diabetes have a mutation in the GLUT 2 gene which means they are unable to make insulin in response to increased blood glucose levels.  GLUT 1 and GLUT 3 are both found everywhere, whereas GLUT 2 is mainly confined to the liver and pancreatic alpha cells.  GLUT 4 is only brought out when exercising for prolonged periods, and is mainly found in skeletal muscle.  I don't think we need to know about GLUT 5, but it's there if you want to look it up! Its low affinity for glucose means it is useful in allowing glucose to diffuse in and out of the beta cell to maintain the intracellular concentration.GLUT2 is also expressed in beta cells, but primarily in the liver, pancreatic alpha cells and brain. GLUT 5 is found in the kidney and reabsorbs glucose in the nephron.   This was in the 'Principles of homeostasis' lecture in case 11. input: Given question: A patient comes into clinic complaining of an inability to move their wrist resulting in a 'wrist drop'. The patient also complains of a loss of sensation in some of the skin in the forearm. What nerve has the patient likely to have damaged? Option A: Median Nerve Option B: Ulnar Nerve Option C: Radial Nerve Option D: Musculocutaneous Nerve Option E: Medial pectoral nerve The correct answer is Option C.
reference: The answer is C - radial nerveThe radial nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the arm (and therefore the wrist) and is the terminal branch of the posterior chord of the brachial plexus - which is damaged in 'wrist drop'A - the median nerve supplies the flexor muscles of the forearm and handB - the ulnar nerve supplies the medial side of the forearmD - the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior armE - the medial pectoral nerve does exist (it innervates the medial side of the chest wall) but it isn't involved in wrist drop This was covered in the upper limb lecture in PCS 3Weeks 4-7: General Surgery (Mr Andrew Shore)Week 4: Introduction to surgical specialitiesWeek 5: OrthopaedicsWeek 6: Plastic and reconstructive surgeryWeek 7: Burns and wound careThese are all really interesting and I found them quite useful to get an overview of the different surgical specialties. I would recommend looking up 'osteotomy' on Wikipedia - it's where they cut a bone and then hold it in place with plates and screws (really cool!)I found the plastic and reconstructive surgery lecture particularly interesting - I had no idea that people could do so much with just tissue! I would highly recommend the documentary 'The Secret Life of Chaos' if you get the chance to watch it - it's not medical related but it's all about the science of randomness and it's amazing!xWeeks 8-10: Psychiatry (Dr Alice Fabbian)Week 8: Introduction to psychiatryWeek 9: Neurophysiology and neuropharmacologyWeek 10: Psychological therapies and counsellingI found these lectures really interesting and it's made me think more about how different illnesses can affect people in different ways. I would definitely recommend reading 'An Unquiet Mind' by Kay Redfield Jamison if you get the chance - it's an account of living with bi-polar disorder from both a patient and doctor perspective. It's really eye opening and a very easy read. I would also recommend watching the film 'A Beautiful Mind' - it's not completely accurate but it gives a good overview of schizophrenia xWeeks 11-12: Revision/practice/catch up on sleepThis is my first year so I'm not sure what we'll be expected to do over the summer but I hope it will mainly be revision! I find making flashcards really helpful - I've made some for all the cases we've had so far and it's really helped to solidify the learning. I'd be happy to share if anyone wants? Also if anyone has any other good revision tips I'd love to hear! Xoxo, Amelia.
best_explanation: Damage to the radial nerve results in a 'wrist drop' in which the patient is unable to lift the wrist. There is also likely to be a loss of sensation in the lateral aspect of the forearm. This is because the radial nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the arm and the lateral aspect of the forearm. The radial nerve also supplies the posterior aspect of the hand, the thumb and the index and middle fingers. As the thumb, index finger and middle finger are mobile the radial nerve is most likely to be damaged in a 'wrist drop'. The ulnar nerve supplies the medial aspect of the forearm and the anterior aspect of the hand. The median nerve supplies the lateral aspect of the forearm, the posterior aspect of the hand and the flexor muscles of the arm. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior aspect of the arm. The medial pectoral nerve supplies the medial aspect of the thorax. The radial nerve is the terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. The ulnar nerve is the terminal branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus. The median nerve is a branch of the medial cord. The musculocutaneous nerve is a branch of the lateral cord. The medial pectoral nerve is a branch of the medial cord.  Information from Moore's Anatomy under Radial Nerve and Brachial Plexus. input: Given question: Martha is suffering from the early stages of heart failure whereby her heart is beginning to be less effective but her neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms mean that she has few symptoms. At a routine check up, her GP notices that her resting heart rate has increased since her last check up, which the GP puts down to this compensatory response. Which of the following neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms is responsible for this increase? Option A: Endothelin pathway activation Option B: Left ventricular hypertrophy Option C: Parasympathetic inhibition Option D: RAAS activation Option E: Sympathetic stimulation The correct answer is Option E.
reference:
A - endothelin pathway activation is responsible for vasoconstriction and reducing perfusionB - left ventricular hypertrophy is a result of the increased afterload placing greater demands on the heart, however it is not responsible for the increase in resting heart rateC - parasympathetic inhibition reduces the heart rate as part of the compensatory mechanismD - RAAS activation will increase the activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system which ultimately increases salt and water retention and increases blood pressureE - sympathetic stimulation increases the resting heart rate in order to increase cardiac output to meet the demands placed upon the heart by the failing heart. This increase in resting heart rate is a fairly reliable predictor of poor prognosis in patients with heart failure. Sources: Kumar and Clark, Dr Yousef's lectures. Learning outcome: describe the neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms that occur in heart failure and their short and long term effects. Link to CASE 2 plenary on Management of Heart Failure. best_explanation: In heart failure, sympathetic stimulation is activated as a compensatory mechanism to raise the resting heart rate.  Endothelin pathway activation is responsible for increasing blood pressure to counteract the reduced ejection fraction.  Parasympathetic inhibition is responsible for decreasing the heart rate to reduce cardiac output.  RAAS activation causes sodium and water retention to increase blood volume.  Left ventricular hypertrophy is a result of the increased workload on the heart and is not a compensatory mechanism.  The increase in resting heart rate is one of the earliest symptoms of heart failure, and is caused by the activation of the sympathetic nervous system. This is in direct contrast to the parasympathetic inhibition that occurs in the body to decrease heart rate in heart failure.  The sympathetic stimulation of the heart causes an increased force of contraction, and the increased afterload places greater demands on the heart to increase its output.  The increased heart rate increases the oxygen demand of the heart, and it is not until this is not met that symptoms start to appear.  At rest, the heart beats slower to save energy, but with exercise the heart rate increases to increase cardiac output.  In heart failure, the heart is unable to increase its cardiac output despite the increase in resting heart rate.  As the heart is unable to increase its output, the increased afterload and oedema (build up of fluid) in the periphentery causes an inability to exercise and leads to the typical symptoms of heart failure.  The increased resting heart rate is therefore a manifestation of the neurohormonal compensatory mechanisms, but is not responsible for increasing the workload on the heart. This workload is increased as the heart cannot increase its output.  Source: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, 9e.  The information in this answer is from the 'The approach to the patient with heart failure' section. input: Given question: A young patient comes into the A&E department with suspected Hirschsprung's disease.  What deficit are they likely to have? Option A: An aganglionic segment of bowel, resulting in an inability of the smooth muscle to contract, thus causing an apparent obstruction due to lack of bowel motility. Option B: An aganglionic segment of bowel, resulting in an inability of the smooth muscle to relax, thus causing bowel obstruction. Option C: A patent ductus arteriosum, resulting in mixing of blood from the right and left sides of the heart causing systemic blood to have less than full oxygenation. Option D: A small, blind-ended pouch of bowel exists in the ileum, within two feet of the ileocaecal junction. Option E: The duodenum is not patent, resulting in an obstruction in the upper gastrointestinal tract. The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Explanation:A - is the cause of Megacolon, a common complication of Hirschprung's disease. It results in a failure of relaxation so the colon cannot be emptied. This causes a build up of faeces and leads to the characteristic features of the disease. B - is the correct answer. C - this is a description of a patent foramen ovale (PFO), a condition which allows unoxygenated blood from the right and left atria to mix. This can be a cause of recurrent stroke. D - this is the description of a Meckel's diverticulum, a common congenital condition where a small pouch of intestine fails to attach properly to the rest of the intestine. E - this describes the cause of a malrotation, where the duodenum has not developed fully so does not lay flat as it should, this can cause an obstruction at the base of the pancreas and also means that the sphincter of oddi is abnormally placed. This can result in pancreatitis and other complications.   This was covered in the case 12 lecture ‘ANORECTAL BLOOD FLOW AND HIERARCHY’.  I tried to make this as confusing as possible, sorry.
======================================================================================================================

Hirschprung's disease is an abnormality in the development of the enteric nervous system. It is a congenital disorder that is believed to occur during embryonic development, when the enteric neurons fail to migrate across the midline of the body. As a result, an aganglionic segment of bowel occurs, meaning there is no motor innervation and hence the bowel cannot contract or relax. This results in an inability to pass meconium and subsequently develop megacolon.   The colon is unable to relax and pass meconium, so the infant quickly becomes constipated. Over time, the colon continues to expand and the wall thickens, stretching the aganglionic segment. In some cases, the colon becomes dilated up to 5 litres, a condition called megalodon. In some cases, the colon passes through the diaphragm (rectal prolapse). Treatment involves cutting out the aganglionic segment and reattaching the healthy ends. Sphincter urethrae traction is often used to pull down a prolapsed rectum.   Source: Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine, 9E. :240-241. Hirschprung's Disease eMedicine  http://www.emedicine.com/ped/topic.cfm?topic=A006378  Malrotation, Meckel's Diverticulum, Duodenal atresia http://www.abdominalatresias.org/malrotation.html  Case 12 Anorectal Blood Flow and Hierarchy.  Normal anorectal blood flow and hierarchy.   The normal pattern of blood supply to the anorectal region is complex and hierarchical. The inferior rectal artery is the most important vessel, but the internal pudenal, superior rectal, and internal hemorrhoidal arteries also contribute. These vessels arise from the anterior trunk of the hypogastric artery, which itself arises from the coeliac trunk. The anterior trunk gives rise to many other vessels that supply the foregut of the body. The blood from these vessels follows the venous system to drain into the inferior vena cava. The regional lymph nodes are found in the inguinal, femoral, and iliac regions. The lymphatic drainage follows the same general route as the blood supply. The nerve supply to the anorectal region is also complex and hierarchical. The pelvic splanchnic nerves, which include the cavernous nerves, the nerves to the external anal canal and external urethral sphincter, the internal urethral sphincter, the perineal branch of the anterior sacral nerve plexus, and the posterior cutaneous cervical nerve, are all important. The nerves arise from the lumbar sympathetic chain. The nerve fibers travel through the paracervical ganglia and then the lumbar sympathetic chain to reach their targets in the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The nerve fibers continue to travel in the paravertebral ganglia and then along the lumbar sympathetic chain to reach the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The n
best_explanation: A: An aganglionic segment of bowel, resulting in an inability of the smooth muscle to contract, thus causing an apparent obstruction due to lack of bowel motility. This is the classic presentation of Hirschprung's disease, usually seen in the context of congenital aganglionic megacolon. The defect usually arises during embryonic development, when the precursor of the enteric nervous system, the splanchnic mesoderm, fails to migrate into the bowel wall.  B: An agglanglionic segment of bowel, resulting in an inability of the smooth muscle to relax, thus causing bowel obstruction. This is the correct answer.  C: A patent ductus arteriosum, resulting in mixing of blood from the right and left sides of the heart causing systemic blood to have less than full oxygenation. This is a product of the foregut not being patent, resulting in mixing of the venous blood. This is a classic presentation of a number of conditions, including transposition of great vessels, and isomerism.  D: A small, blind-ended pouch of bowel exists in the ileum, within two feet of the ileocaecal junction. This is the description of a Meckel's diverticulum, which usually arises post embryonic development, as the ectodermal tissue that fails to integrate with the bowel wall is in the ileum, usually 2 feet from the ileocaecal junction.  E: The duodenum is not patent, resulting in an obstruction in the upper gastrointestinal tract. This is the result of the midgut not being patent, resulting in obstruction of the upper GI tract.
